properties.name: OBSERVED 2026-09-29: three fix agents sharing one CARGO_TARGET_DIR across three git worktrees. A build in one worktree linked a reflow2-core built from ANOTHER worktree's source, and failed with "cannot find function `name_leads_with_open` in crate `reflow2_core`". A result taken in a shared target dir may not be testing the worktree it ran in
properties.source: dev_reflow2 hub session, 2026-09-29 (fix agent R-B's report)
properties.statement:
SETUP (dev_reflow2 hub, fix program for art:dev-reflow2-two-agent-exercise-feedback-2026-09-29). Three agents each worked in their own worktree off origin/main. To compile RocksDB only once on a 4-core, 11 GB box, all three used ONE CARGO_TARGET_DIR. The shared first build took about 60 minutes. The shared directory was the hub session's instruction.

OBSERVED: `cargo build -p reflow2-mcp --bin reflow2-mcp` in one worktree failed with "cannot find function `name_leads_with_open` in crate `reflow2_core`". That function exists in that worktree's own core source, so the rlib it linked had been built from another worktree.

THE REPORTING AGENT'S EXPLANATION, not independently verified: cargo gives a workspace crate the same artifact slot in every checkout, because its metadata hash uses the path relative to the workspace. Freshness is then judged from dep-info that names the OTHER worktree's source files. This is a hypothesis about cargo internals; nobody has measured it here.

CONSEQUENCE, which holds whatever the mechanism: a pass or a failure taken in a shared target dir may be testing another worktree's code, and it can do so silently. A link error is only the loud case. So failing-first observations taken that way cannot be cited.

WORKAROUND NOW IN USE, not a verified fix:
- every cargo command against the shared dir runs under one flock;
- inside the lock, `cargo clean -p reflow2-core -p reflow2-mcp` runs before the build, keeping the dependency artifacts;
- core-only runs (`--no-default-features`, no RocksDB) use a private target dir per worktree;
- every result taken before the change is being re-run.
The clean fix is a target dir per worktree, at the cost of one RocksDB compile each; ~34 min release and ~60 min debug were measured here.

RELATED: fact:a-worktree-fix-recorded-its-design-changes-in-the-live-store-and-the-branch-gate-failed-2026-09-22 is the design-record half of the same situation: parallel worktrees beside a live shared server. Nothing in AGENTS.md or cap:parallel-work warns about the build-directory half.

ADDED THE SAME DAY: a second shared-state hazard across worktrees, the git STASH.

OBSERVED: for a failing-first run, one agent stashed its source changes in its worktree while another agent stashed its own in a different worktree. The first agent's `git stash pop` then applied the OTHER agent's changes into its own worktree. The stash ref lives in the repository's common directory, so every worktree sees one stash list, and `pop` takes whichever entry is on top.

The same list also held two entries belonging to OTHER sessions working on the repo (an export snapshot, and a perf branch "awaiting Anthony's ship/hold"). A careless pop there would have applied another session's parked work.

Repaired by the agent that noticed:
- the other agent's changes were re-stashed under an explicit label;
- its own entry was applied by SHA and dropped.

The rule the fix agents now follow: no `git stash` in parallel worktrees. For failing-first, use a patch file (`git diff > f.patch`, `git checkout -- paths`, `git apply`), or a separate detached worktree at origin/main.

Neither hazard is named in AGENTS.md, COORD.md or cap:parallel-work.

WHAT PARALLEL FIX WORK COSTS ON THIS BOX, measured 2026-09-29 (4 cores, 11 GB, three reflow2 agents plus one flo2 agent at once, the lock protocol adopted mid-way). Wall-clock time from brief to merged PR, including CI:
- flo2 fix PRs (TypeScript, no Rust build): 25 minutes for both.
- reflow2 #625: about 3.9 h, 277 tool calls.
- reflow2 #624: about 4.7 h, 165 tool calls.
- reflow2 #623: over 4 h and still merging at the time of writing.
- The first shared debug build took about 60 minutes.
- Two of the three reflow2 agents hit the harness's 200-turn limit and had to be resumed.
- CI's workspace job took about 20 minutes per run.
So on this box a reflow2 fix package costs half a working day, and the build lock, not the code, sets the pace.
